questions.q: What is the key difference between a Dynamic Management View (DMV) and a Dynamic Management Function (DMF)?
options: A DMV is queried directly with SELECT; a DMF takes a parameter and is called via CROSS APPLY or OUTER APPLY
A DMV only works in Azure SQL Database, while a DMF only works on-premises
A DMF returns data permanently logged to disk, while a DMV is always in-memory only
There is no functional difference — the names are interchangeable
questions.explain: DMVs are queried directly (SELECT * FROM sys.dm_exec_requests); DMFs take a parameter, typically a handle from a DMV, and are called with CROSS APPLY.

questions.q: What does the sys.dm_os_* prefix generally indicate about a DMV?
options: It covers operating-system-level data such as wait stats, memory, and performance counters
It covers only database-level metadata like table and column definitions
It is reserved exclusively for security auditing views
It only applies to DMVs available in SQL Server 2008 and earlier
questions.explain: sys.dm_os_* views expose OS-level and engine-level data: wait stats, schedulers, memory clerks, performance counters.

questions.q: Which DMV returns one row per currently executing request, including its wait type and elapsed time?
options: sys.dm_exec_requests
sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats
sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats
sys.databases
questions.explain: sys.dm_exec_requests is the core DMV for seeing what is actively executing right now.

questions.q: Why would you call sys.dm_exec_sql_text() with CROSS APPLY against sys.dm_exec_requests instead of querying it alone?
options: Because sys.dm_exec_sql_text is a DMF that needs a sql_handle as input, and sys.dm_exec_requests supplies that handle for each active request
Because CROSS APPLY is required syntax for every catalog view query
Because sys.dm_exec_sql_text cannot be queried under any circumstances
Because sys.dm_exec_requests deletes rows once they are read
questions.explain: DMFs like sys.dm_exec_sql_text take a parameter (sql_handle) rather than returning all rows on their own, so they're applied per-row against a DMV that supplies that handle.

questions.q: What happens to the counters in sys.dm_os_wait_stats when the SQL Server service restarts?
options: They reset to zero, since DMV data reflects a live snapshot rather than a permanent historical log
They are automatically archived to msdb before the restart
They continue accumulating from where they left off
They are copied into sys.databases for permanent storage
questions.explain: DMV data like wait stats is cumulative only since the last restart (or manual clear) — it is not a durable log.
